questions.prompt: What is the right starting point for choosing a design pattern?

options.text: The problem's forces and the matching pattern's intent
Browsing the catalog for a pattern that looks interesting
Whichever pattern you used most recently
The pattern with the most classes

questions.explanation: Start from the problem, use the category as a map, and match by intent — not by scanning the catalog for something to apply.

questions.prompt: The principle warning against building flexibility for imagined future needs is abbreviated ____.
questions.explanation: YAGNI — 'You Aren't Gonna Need It' — cautions against speculative complexity, including speculatively applied patterns.

options.text: Over-applying one favorite pattern to every problem
Using the fastest possible algorithm
Writing code with no patterns at all
Refactoring too rarely

questions.explanation: The Golden Hammer forces a familiar pattern everywhere — 'if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail.'

options.text: Write simple code first and introduce a pattern when a real recurring pressure appears
Always start every class from a pattern template
Remove all patterns during refactoring
Apply every pattern preemptively to be safe

questions.explanation: Patterns are destinations you refactor toward once a genuine pressure emerges, not starting templates.

questions.prompt: Which of these are patterns that live BEYOND the 23 Gang of Four patterns? Select all that apply.

options.text: MVC (Model-View-Controller)
Dependency Injection
Repository
Observer

questions.explanation: MVC, DI, and Repository are architectural/enterprise patterns (or a technique, for DI). Observer is one of the 23 GoF patterns.

questions.prompt: Why can a design pattern sometimes be unnecessary in TypeScript?

options.text: Language features (first-class functions, built-in iterators) can provide the pattern's end directly
TypeScript forbids design patterns
Patterns only work in Java
TypeScript automatically applies all 23 patterns

questions.explanation: As Norvig noted, many GoF patterns are simpler or invisible in higher-level languages — e.g. Strategy/Command as functions, Iterator built in.
